options.summary: Use extended regular expressions (no backslashes before ( ) + ?)
options.description: Interpret regular expressions as extended (modern) regular expressions rather than basic regular expressions (BRE's). The re_format(7) manual page fully describes both formats.

options.summary: The files listed as parameters for the "w" functions are created (or truncated) before any processing begins, by default.
options.description: The files listed as parameters for the "w" functions are created (or truncated) before any processing begins, by default. The -a option causes sed to delay opening each file until a command containing the related "w" function is applied to a line of input.

options.description: Append the editing commands found in the file command_file to the list of commands. The editing commands should each be listed on a separate line. The commands are read from the standard input if command_file is "-".

options.summary: Edit files in-place, saving backups with the specified extension.
options.description:
Edit files in-place, saving backups with the specified extension. If a zero-length extension is given, no backup will be saved. It is not recommended to give a zero-length extension when in-place editing files, as you risk corruption or partial content in situations where disk space is exhausted, etc.

Note that in-place editing with -I still takes place in a single continuous line address space covering all files, although each file preserves its individuality instead of forming one output stream. The line counter is never reset between files, address ranges can span file boundaries, and the "$" address matches only the last line of the last file. (See Sed Addresses.) That can lead to unexpected results in many cases of in-place editing, where using -i is desired.

options.summary: Edit files in place; the backup suffix argument is required ('' for none)
options.description: Edit files in-place similarly to -I, but treat each file independently from other files. In particular, line numbers in each file start at 1, the "$" address matches the last line of the current file, and address ranges are limited to the current file. (See Sed Addresses.) The net result is as though each file were edited by a separate sed instance.

examples.description: Edit a file in place without keeping a backup
Edit in place and keep the original as path/to/file.bak

options.summary: Only print lines the script prints explicitly (with p)
options.description: By default, each line of input is echoed to the standard output after all of the commands have been applied to it. The -n option suppresses this behavior.
